claim: A complex of NuMA and dynein/dynactin is required for robust spindle orientation in a number of cell types.
source: A complex of NuMA and dynein/dynactin is required for robust spindle orientation in a number of cell types.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous research throughout the manuscript.

claim: Previous research proposed that cortical dynein/dynactin was sufficient to generate forces on astral microtubules (MTs) to orient the spindle, with NuMA acting as a passive tether.
source: Previous research proposed that cortical dynein/dynactin was sufficient to generate forces on astral microtubules (MTs) to orient the spindle, with NuMA acting as a passive tether.
evidence: This claim references previous research models and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Dynein/dynactin is insufficient for spindle orientation establishment in keratinocytes.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that dynein/dynactin is insufficient for spindle orientation establishment in keratinocytes and that NuMA's MT-binding domain, which targets MT tips, is also required.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments showing that cortical dynein/dynactin localization is maintained in NuMAΔMTBD cells, yet spindle orientation is defective (Figure 3F,G).

claim: NuMA's MT-binding domain, which targets MT tips, is required for spindle orientation.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that dynein/dynactin is insufficient for spindle orientation establishment in keratinocytes and that NuMA's MT-binding domain, which targets MT tips, is also required.
evidence: This is supported by data showing spindle orientation defects in NuMAΔMTBD cells (Figure 3D,E).

claim: Loss of NuMA-MT interactions in skin caused defects in spindle orientation and epidermal differentiation, leading to neonatal lethality.
source: Loss of NuMA-MT interactions in skin caused defects in spindle orientation and epidermal differentiation, leading to neonatal lethality.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data showing spindle orientation defects (Figure 3J,K), differentiation defects (Figure 5B-I), and neonatal lethality (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: NuMA-MT interactions are required in adult mice for hair follicle morphogenesis and spindle orientation within the transit-amplifying cells of the matrix.
source: In addition, we show that NuMA-MT interactions are also required in adult mice for hair follicle morphogenesis and spindle orientation within the transit-amplifying cells of the matrix.
evidence: This is supported by data showing hair growth defects (Figure 6C,F) and spindle orientation defects in matrix cells (Figure 6G,H).

claim: Loss of spindle orientation in matrix cells results in defective differentiation of matrix-derived lineages.
source: Loss of spindle orientation in matrix cells results in defective differentiation of matrix-derived lineages.
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of hair shaft and inner root sheath markers in mutant follicles (Figure 6O-R).

claim: NuMA contains a domain that directly interacts with MTs.
source: In addition to its ability to recruit dynein/dynactin to the cell cortex, NuMA contains a domain that directly interacts with MTs (Du et al., 2002; Haren and Merdes, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and confirmed by in vitro binding assays (Figure 2I-K).

claim: NuMA's MT-binding domain (MTBD) is conserved among flies, worms, and mammals.
source: This MT-binding domain (MTBD) is conserved among flies, worms, and mammals and has been characterized to stabilize and bundle MTs.
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge from previous research.

claim: NuMA's MTBD has been characterized to stabilize and bundle MTs.
source: This MT-binding domain (MTBD) is conserved among flies, worms, and mammals and has been characterized to stabilize and bundle MTs.
evidence: This is based on previous characterization studies and is also observed in this study at high expression levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: NuMA localizes to microtubule tips.
source: NuMA localizes to microtubule tips
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence showing GFP-NuMA-TIP at MT tips (Figure 1B,C,G) and endogenous NuMA at MT tips (Figure 2A,B).

claim: A region of NuMA spanning the linker domain to the MTBD localizes to MT tips.
source: Thus, a region of NuMA spanning the linker domain (which follows the 4.1-binding domain) to the MTBD localizes to MT tips.
evidence: This is demonstrated by localization studies of various NuMA constructs (Figure 1B-F).

claim: NuMA-TIP and Eb1 only very rarely colocalized on the same MT tip.
source: However, co-staining revealed that NuMA-TIP and Eb1 only very rarely colocalized on the same MT tip (Figure 1H,K,K' <2% of MTs, n = 200).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-staining experiments quantifying colocalization.

claim: NuMA-TIP localized specifically to both MT plus and minus ends following treatment with nocodazole.
source: In stark contrast, NuMA-TIP localized specifically to both MT plus and minus ends following treatment with nocodazole (Figure 1I,K',K'').
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence of nocodazole-treated cells (Figure 1I,K',K'').

claim: Eb1 was displaced from the tip and labeled the MT lattice upon nocodazole addition.
source: This was in contrast to Eb1, which was displaced from the tip and labeled the MT lattice upon nocodazole addition (Figure 1K'').
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence showing Eb1 localization after nocodazole treatment (Figure 1K'').

claim: NuMA-TIP clearly favors binding to MT ends over MT sides.
source: Since nocodazole significantly decreased the density of MTs and helped resolve MT ends, this treatment revealed that NuMA-TIP clearly favors binding to MT ends over MT sides.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NuMA-TIP localizes to MT ends after nocodazole treatment (Figure 1I,K',K'').

claim: A higher percentage of vinblastine-treated cells showed MT tip localization of NuMA-TIP when compared with DMSO-treated cells.
source: We found that a higher percentage of vinblastine-treated cells showed MT tip localization of NuMA-TIP when compared with DMSO-treated cells, while taxol treatment resulted in a significant loss of MT tip localization (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitation of NuMA-TIP localization under different drug treatments (Figure 1J).

claim: Taxol treatment resulted in a significant loss of MT tip localization of NuMA-TIP.
source: We found that a higher percentage of vinblastine-treated cells showed MT tip localization of NuMA-TIP when compared with DMSO-treated cells, while taxol treatment resulted in a significant loss of MT tip localization (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitation showing decreased NuMA-TIP tip localization with taxol (Figure 1J).

claim: NuMA preferentially recognizes flayed MT ends over straight ends.
source: This suggests that NuMA preferentially recognizes flayed MT ends over straight ends and is consistent with a report that NuMA interacts preferentially with vinblastine-induced curled MTs over taxol-stabilized MTs (Volkov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the drug treatment experiments and supported by a citation to Volkov et al., 2015.

claim: Endogenous NuMA exhibited MT tip localization in early prometaphase.
source: Endogenous NuMA also exhibited MT tip localization. In early prometaphase, before NuMA had strongly accumulated at both the spindle poles and the cortex, we noted discrete puncta at MT tips (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence of endogenous NuMA in early prometaphase cells (Figure 2A).

claim: Briefly treating cells with nocodazole resulted in enhanced tip localization of endogenous NuMA.
source: Briefly treating cells with nocodazole resulted in enhanced tip localization (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence of nocodazole-treated cells (Figure 2B).

claim: MT-tip binding is a property of full-length endogenous NuMA.
source: Thus, MT-tip binding is a property of full-length endogenous NuMA.
evidence: This is inferred from observations of endogenous NuMA localization at MT tips (Figure 2A,B).

claim: The NuMA-TIP region is both necessary and sufficient for NuMA's MT tip interactions.
source: This region is therefore both necessary and sufficient for NuMA's MT tip interactions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by localization studies of NuMA deletion constructs (Figure 2D-F).

claim: Deletion of the MTBD domain alone compromises tip-localization.
source: Importantly, deletion of the MTBD domain alone (which keeps the LGN-binding domain intact) compromises tip-localization (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by localization analysis of NuMAΔMTBD construct (Figure 2E).

claim: A NuMA mutant harboring a MTBD domain deletion allows testing the role of MT tip-binding activity during spindle orientation without disrupting other critical domains of NuMA.
source: Therefore, a NuMA mutant harboring a MTBD domain deletion allows us to test the role of MT tip-binding activity during spindle orientation without disrupting other critical domains of NuMA that are known to be required for its cortical localization.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the domain structure and localization properties of the mutant.

claim: Many of the brighter NuMA-TIP puncta were stationary, consistent with NuMA-TIP's role in stabilizing MTs.
source: Many of the brighter puncta were stationary, consistent with NuMA-TIP's role in stabilizing MTs.
evidence: This is observed in time-lapse imaging experiments (Figure 2G,H).

claim: Motile GFP puncta tracking toward the cell periphery along MT plus tips were observed.
source: In addition, we observed motile GFP puncta tracking toward the cell periphery along MT plus tips (Figure 2G,H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging (Figure 2G,H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: NuMA-TIP puncta remained localized to the ends of depolymerizing MTs.
source: Furthermore, these puncta remained localized to the ends of depolymerizing MTs.
evidence: This is observed in time-lapse imaging experiments (Figure 2G,H).

claim: NuMA can remain attached to both growing and shrinking MT ends.
source: These data demonstrate that NuMA can remain attached to both growing and shrinking MT ends and suggests that this may be functionally important for facilitating the interactions of astral MT tips with the cell cortex during spindle orientation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging showing NuMA-TIP on both growing and shrinking MTs (Figure 2G,H).

claim: NuMA-TIP is sufficient for direct interaction with MT ends.
source: While these data cannot rule out roles for accessory proteins in modulating NuMA's association with MTs, they do demonstrate that NuMA-TIP is sufficient for direct interaction with MT ends.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro binding assays with purified NuMA-TIP protein (Figure 2I-K).

claim: Loss of the MTBD did not impair localization of NuMA to either the spindle poles or cell cortex.
source: Loss of the MTBD did not impair localization of NuMA to either the spindle poles or cell cortex; however, it did cause a defect in spindle orientation (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence showing normal NuMAΔMTBD localization (Figure 3B).

claim: Loss of the MTBD caused a defect in spindle orientation in cultured keratinocytes.
source: Loss of the MTBD did not impair localization of NuMA to either the spindle poles or cell cortex; however, it did cause a defect in spindle orientation (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitation of spindle angles showing randomization in NuMAΔMTBD cells (Figure 3E).

claim: More than 80% of control cells had spindles oriented within 30 degrees of the center of the cortical NuMA crescent.
source: More than 80% of control cells had spindles oriented within 30 degrees of the center of the cortical NuMA crescent (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitation of spindle angles in control cells (Figure 3D).

claim: NuMAΔMTBD cells showed a complete randomization of division orientation.
source: In contrast, NuMAΔMTBD cells showed a complete randomization of division orientation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by radial histogram showing random spindle angles (Figure 3E).

claim: NuMAΔMTBD acts as a dominant-negative allele.
source: Similar results were found by overexpressing NuMAΔMTBD-GFP in wild-type keratinocytes, demonstrating that this acts as a dominant-negative allele (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spindle orientation defects upon overexpression of NuMAΔMTBD-GFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: NuMA-MT interactions are essential for proper mitotic spindle orientation establishment in cultured keratinocytes.
source: These data demonstrate that NuMA-MT interactions are essential for proper mitotic spindle orientation establishment in cultured keratinocytes.
evidence: This is concluded from the spindle orientation defects observed in NuMAΔMTBD cells (Figure 3D,E).

claim: p150glued of the dynactin complex co-localized with the cortical crescents of both NuMA and NuMAΔMTBD.
source: We found that p150glued of the dynactin complex co-localized with the cortical crescents of both NuMA and NuMAΔMTBD (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunofluorescence of NuMA and p150glued (Figure 3F,G).

claim: This co-localization was true in 100% of cells examined (n = 50 from two experiments).
source: This was true in 100% of cells examined (n = 50 from two experiments).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative result from the experiments.

claim: Knockdown of NuMA resulted in an almost complete loss of cortical dynactin.
source: In contrast, we recently published that knockdown of NuMA resulted in an almost complete loss of cortical dynactin (Seldin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: Cortical recruitment of dynein/dynactin is not sufficient for proper spindle orientation.
source: These data demonstrate that cortical recruitment of dynein/dynactin is not sufficient for proper spindle orientation and that NuMA's MTBD provides an essential additional function.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that NuMAΔMTBD maintains cortical dynein/dynactin but still has spindle orientation defects (Figure 3F,G,E).

claim: NuMA's MTBD provides an essential additional function for spindle orientation beyond dynein/dynactin recruitment.
source: These data demonstrate that cortical recruitment of dynein/dynactin is not sufficient for proper spindle orientation and that NuMA's MTBD provides an essential additional function.
evidence: This is concluded from the spindle orientation defects in NuMAΔMTBD cells despite normal dynein/dynactin localization.

claim: Mitotic spindles in situ align either parallel to the basement membrane to generate two basal progenitors, or perpendicular to it to generate one basal progenitor and one suprabasal cell that will differentiate.
source: In contrast to cultured keratinocytes, mitotic spindles in situ align either parallel to the basement membrane to generate two basal progenitors, or perpendicular to it to generate one basal progenitor and one suprabasal cell that will differentiate (Lechler and Fuchs, 2005; Poulson and Lechler, 2010; Smart, 1970).
evidence: This is stated based on previous research cited.

claim: The mutant form of NuMA localized normally to spindle poles and the cortex of mitotic cells in embryonic tissue sections.
source: We analyzed NuMA localization in embryonic tissue sections and confirmed that the mutant form localized normally to spindle poles and the cortex of mitotic cells, consistent with our findings in cultured cells (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence of tissue sections (Figure 3H,I).

claim: Controls showed a bimodal distribution of spindle orientations.
source: In agreement with previous studies, controls showed a bimodal distribution of orientations (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by radial histogram of spindle angles in control epidermis (Figure 3J).

claim: Quantitation of spindle angles in mutant epidermis showed a dramatic decrease in perpendicular spindles coupled with an increase in oblique and parallel spindles.
source: Quantitation of spindle angles in mutant epidermis showed a dramatic decrease in perpendicular spindles coupled with an increase in oblique and parallel spindles (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by radial histogram of spindle angles in mutant epidermis (Figure 3K).

claim: The spindle orientation defect was not an indirect effect of loss of polarity or cell death.
source: This defect was not an indirect effect of loss of polarity or cell death, as both the Golgi and centrosomes showed proper polarization and cleaved caspase 3-positive cells did not significantly increase in number (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence showing normal Golgi polarization and no increase in apoptosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).

claim: The randomized spindle angles observed in NuMAΔMTBD mice are likely due to the maintenance of cortical dynein, which cannot efficiently orient the spindle in the absence of NuMA-MT interactions.
source: The randomized spindle angles observed in NuMAΔMTBD mice are likely due to the maintenance of cortical dynein, which cannot efficiently orient the spindle in the absence of NuMA-MT interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with NuMA knockdown mice and the observation that cortical dynein is maintained in NuMAΔMTBD mice.

claim: Loss of NuMA does not cause mitotic spindle assembly defects in cultured keratinocytes, mammalian epidermis or fly neuroblasts.
source: Loss of NuMA does not cause mitotic spindle assembly defects in cultured keratinocytes, mammalian epidermis or fly neuroblasts (Bowman et al., 2006; Seldin et al., 2013; Siller et al., 2006; Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on previous research cited.

claim: Previous analysis of NuMAΔMTBD mice harboring a full body deletion suggested that this region was essential for development and that cultured mutant fibroblasts had mitotic spindle defects.
source: However, previous analysis of NuMAΔMTBD mice harboring a full body deletion suggested that this region was essential for development and that cultured mutant fibroblasts had mitotic spindle defects (Silk et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated based on a previous publication cited.

claim: No defects were detected in mitotic morphology, stage, or number in mutant keratinocytes.
source: We did not detect any defects in mitotic morphology, stage, or number in mutant keratinocytes (Figure 4A–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of mitotic cells showing normal morphology and distribution (Figure 4A-G).

claim: Metaphase and anaphase spindles exhibited normal morphology in NuMAΔMTBD keratinocytes.
source: Metaphase and anaphase spindles exhibited normal morphology (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence images (Figure 4A,B).

claim: The localization of NuMA to the cell cortex, the incidence of abnormal spindles and the extent of mis-aligned DNA were all similar between control and NuMAΔMTBD cells.
source: The localization of NuMA to the cell cortex, the incidence of abnormal spindles and the extent of mis-aligned DNA were all similar between control and NuMAΔMTBD cells (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitation of various mitotic parameters (Figure 4C-F).

claim: There were no significant differences in the percentage of cells in different mitotic stages or their spindle lengths between control and NuMAΔMTBD cells.
source: There were also no significant differences in the percentage of cells in different mitotic stages or their spindle lengths (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitation (Figure 4F,G).

claim: Flow cytometry analysis of mutant epidermal cells revealed no evidence of aneuploidy or polyploidy.
source: Furthermore, flow cytometry analysis of mutant epidermal cells revealed no evidence of aneuploidy or polyploidy (Figure 4I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data (Figure 4I,J).

claim: The phenotype observed is distinct from those caused by mutations in mitotic regulators, arguing against an underlying mitotic defect.
source: Finally, the phenotype that we observed is distinct from those caused by mutations in mitotic regulators, arguing against an underlying mitotic defect (Foijer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with known mitotic defect phenotypes and supported by a citation.

claim: The data are consistent with previous studies on cultured keratinocytes, mouse epidermis and fly neuroblasts.
source: Nevertheless, it should be noted that our data are consistent with previous studies on cultured keratinocytes, mouse epidermis and fly neuroblasts (Bowman et al., 2006; Seldin et al., 2013; Siller et al., 2006; Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with previous research.

claim: There were no significant differences in the number of astral MTs per spindle pole between control and NuMAΔMTBD keratinocytes.
source: Considering that spindle orientation defects could result from compromised astral MT integrity, we also quantified the number of astral MTs in both control and NuMAΔMTBD mice and found no significant differences (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitation (Figure 4H).

claim: Loss of NuMA's MTBD causes spindle orientation defects but not spindle assembly defects.
source: Having established that loss of NuMA's MTBD causes spindle orientation defects but not spindle assembly defects, we sought to determine the resulting consequences on epidermal development.
evidence: This is concluded from the data showing spindle orientation defects without mitotic defects (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: Mice with epidermal loss of NuMA's MTBD were neonatal lethal.
source: Mice with epidermal loss of NuMA's MTBD were neonatal lethal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Neonatal lethality was associated with a mild barrier defect.
source: This lethality was associated with a mild barrier defect, as observed by an X-gal penetration assay (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by X-gal penetration assay (Figure 5A).

claim: In control mice, keratin 5/14 marked a monolayer of proliferative basal cells, while keratin 10 was present in their differentiated progeny.
source: In control mice, keratin 5/14 marked a monolayer of proliferative basal cells, while keratin 10 was present in their differentiated progeny (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence (Figure 5B).

claim: In mutant mice, an expansion of K5/14-positive cells into suprabasal layers and their mixing with K10-positive cells was observed.
source: In mutant mice, we observed an expansion of K5/14- positive cells into suprabasal layers and their mixing with K10-positive cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence (Figure 5C).

claim: These defects were noticed as early as e16.5, before epidermal barrier activity is fully established.
source: These defects were noticed as early as e16.5, before epidermal barrier activity is fully established (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence at e16.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: Later differentiation markers, such as loricrin and filaggrin, were present at much lower levels in mutant skin.
source: Later differentiation markers, such as loricrin and filaggrin, were present at much lower levels in mutant skin, explaining in part the compromised barrier and neonatal lethality (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and Western blot (Figure 5D-F).

claim: There was a dramatic upregulation of the stress marker keratin 6 in mutant skin.
source: There was also a dramatic upregulation of the stress marker keratin 6 in mutant skin (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and Western blot (Figure 5G-I).

claim: Increased numbers of cycling cells in the mutant suprabasal epidermis were observed by both BrdU and phospho-histone H3 staining.
source: Consistent with a differentiation defect, we observed increased numbers of cycling cells in the mutant suprabasal epidermis by both BrdU and phospho-histone H3 staining (Figure 5J–P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BrdU incorporation and phospho-histone H3 staining (Figure 5J-P).

claim: An increase in basal cell proliferation was noted, which is likely a consequence of barrier dysfunction.
source: In addition, we noted an increase in basal cell proliferation, which is likely a consequence of barrier dysfunction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased basal proliferation in the context of barrier defects.

claim: Analysis of e16.5 epidermis revealed an increase in suprabasal cell divisions, but not in basal divisions.
source: In support of this, analysis of e16.5 epidermis (a stage at which the barrier is just beginning to form) revealed an increase in suprabasal cell divisions, but not in basal divisions (Figure 5N).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitation of phospho-histone H3 positive cells at e16.5 (Figure 5N).

claim: High levels of spindle misorientation are not tolerated and the oblique divisions observed cannot promote proper differentiation of the epidermis.
source: These studies demonstrate that high levels of spindle misorientation are not tolerated and that the oblique divisions observed cannot promote proper differentiation of the epidermis.
evidence: This is concluded from the differentiation defects and lethality observed in NuMAΔMTBD mice.

claim: Previous data suggested that low levels of spindle misorientation were not detrimental to epidermal development.
source: Previous data suggested that low levels of spindle misorientation were not detrimental to epidermal development (Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on a previous publication cited.

claim: There appears to be a critical threshold at which a decrease in functionally asymmetric divisions impairs development.
source: Therefore, there appears to be a critical threshold at which a decrease in functionally asymmetric divisions impairs development.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the current results with previous studies showing tolerance of low levels of misorientation.

claim: The NuMAΔMTBD mouse line serves as an invaluable tool that allows specific addressing of the role of spindle orientation in a tissue context.
source: The NuMAΔMTBD mouse line therefore serves as an invaluable tool that allows us to specifically address the role of spindle orientation in a tissue context.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the properties of the mouse line.

claim: Previously, it has not been possible to specifically perturb spindle orientation during postnatal hair morphogenesis.
source: Previously, it has not been possible to specifically perturb spindle orientation during postnatal hair morphogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: The hair follicle is a highly organized epidermal appendage that undergoes cycles of growth, regression and rest throughout an animal's lifetime.
source: The hair follicle is a highly organized epidermal appendage that undergoes cycles of growth, regression and rest throughout an animal's lifetime.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about hair follicles.

claim: The growth phase, called anagen, is responsible for producing the fully differentiated hair shaft.
source: The growth phase, called anagen, is responsible for producing the fully differentiated hair shaft.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the hair cycle.

claim: Three proliferative compartments of the hair follicle, the bulge stem cells, the outer root sheath (ORS) and the transit-amplifying matrix cells, are responsible for generating the cell types that make up the mature hair follicle.
source: Three proliferative compartments of the hair follicle, the bulge stem cells, the outer root sheath (ORS) and the transit-amplifying matrix cells, are responsible for generating the cell types that make up the mature hair follicle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about hair follicle structure.

claim: An almost complete absence of hair regrowth was observed in the mutant mice.
source: In contrast to the robust hair regrowth seen in littermates, we observed an almost complete absence of hair regrowth in the mutant mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by photographs of shaved mice (Figure 6C).

claim: Matrix cells are keratin 14-negative.
source: While bulge and ORS cells are contiguous with the interfollicular basal layer and express keratin 14, matrix cells are keratin 14-negative.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about matrix cell markers.

claim: Krt14-NuMA-GFP expression was sufficient to fully rescue the neonatal lethality caused by embryonic loss of NuMA's MTBD.
source: Krt14-NuMA-GFP expression was sufficient to fully rescue the neonatal lethality caused by embryonic loss of NuMA's MTBD (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by photographs of viable mice (Figure 6E).

claim: MatrixΔMTBD mice displayed severe hair growth defects, indicating a critical role for NuMA's MTBD in matrix cells.
source: However, these mice displayed severe hair growth defects, indicating a critical role for NuMA's MTBD in matrix cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by photographs showing hair loss (Figure 6F).

claim: The small tufts of backskin hair present at early stages in matrixΔMTBD mice was lost during subsequent hair cycles.
source: The small tufts of backskin hair present at early stages in matrixΔMTBD mice was lost during subsequent hair cycles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by photographs at different time points (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: The spindles of matrix cells lacking NuMA's MTBD exhibited a randomization of orientations.
source: Compared with controls, the spindles of matrix cells lacking NuMA's MTBD exhibited a randomization of orientations (similar to the orientation pattern seen in knockout interfollicular epidermis), demonstrating that the MTBD is critical for robust spindle positioning within this cellular compartment (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by radial histograms of spindle angles (Figure 6G,H).

claim: Keratins 5 and 6 mark the ORS and companion layer of the hair follicle, respectively, and demonstrated similar staining patterns in control and mutant follicles.
source: Keratins 5 and 6 mark the ORS and companion layer of the hair follicle, respectively, and demonstrated similar staining patterns in control and mutant follicles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence (Figure 6I-L).

claim: The matrix marker P-cadherin showed normal staining in both control and mutants, indicating that the matrix population was properly specified.
source: Additionally, the matrix marker P-cadherin showed normal staining in both control and mutants, indicating that the matrix population was properly specified (Figure 6I–N).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence (Figure 6I-N).

claim: AE13 and GATA3, which mark the hair shaft and inner root sheath (IRS) cells (all matrix descendants), respectively, were decreased and/or disorganized in the mutant follicles.
source: In contrast, AE13 and GATA3, which mark the hair shaft and inner root sheath (IRS) cells (all matrix descendants), respectively, were decreased and/or disorganized in the mutant follicles (Figure 6O–R).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence (Figure 6O-R).

claim: Robust spindle orientation is necessary for the proper differentiation of matrix progeny.
source: Therefore, robust spindle orientation is necessary for the proper differentiation of matrix progeny.
evidence: This is concluded from the loss of differentiation markers in mutant follicles with spindle orientation defects.

claim: The matrix-derived hair shaft and IRS cell lineages are lost when BMP signaling is inhibited.
source: Notably, the matrix-derived hair shaft and IRS cell lineages are also lost when BMP signaling is inhibited (Andl et al., 2004; Kobielak et al., 2003; Kulessa et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated based on previous research cited.

claim: BMP signaling is one of the earliest detectable steps in the differentiation of hair shaft and IRS lineages.
source: In fact, BMP signaling is one of the earliest detectable steps in the differentiation of these lineages.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about hair follicle differentiation.

claim: Analysis of BMP activity using anti-pSMAD1/5 antibodies revealed a loss of signaling in mutant follicles.
source: Analysis of BMP activity using anti-pSMAD1/5 antibodies revealed a loss of signaling (Figure 6S,T).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence (Figure 6S,T).

claim: These data are consistent with BMP signaling acting downstream of these asymmetric divisions.
source: These data are consistent with BMP signaling acting downstream of these asymmetric divisions.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of BMP signaling when spindle orientation is disrupted.

claim: Examination of older mice revealed additional phenotypic similarities with mice in which BMP signaling was blocked, including cyst formation and aberrant spatial localization of follicular proliferation.
source: Examination of older mice revealed additional phenotypic similarities with mice in which BMP signaling was blocked, including cyst formation and aberrant spatial localization of follicular proliferation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and histology (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).

claim: Matrix-derived cells in the mutant mice lacked markers for IRS and hair shaft but appeared to be non-proliferative, as judged by lack of BrdU incorporation.
source: Although matrix-derived cells in the mutant mice lacked markers for IRS and hair shaft, they appeared to be non-proliferative, as judged by lack of BrdU incorporation (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by BrdU staining (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).

claim: A spindle orientation-dependent event is required to activate BMP signaling.
source: Our data demonstrate that a spindle orientation-dependent event is also required to activate BMP signaling, which is therefore not simply driven by compartmentalization.
evidence: This is concluded from the loss of BMP signaling in cells with disrupted spindle orientation.

claim: NuMA has a new role in addition to being important for the recruitment of dynein/dynactin to the cortex.
source: Here, we have documented a new role for NuMA, one of the core components of the spindle orientation machinery. In addition to being important for the recruitment of dynein/dynactin to the cortex, we have found that NuMA's dynein-independent interactions with MTs are also essential for spindle orientation.
evidence: This is concluded from the data showing that NuMA-MT interactions are required for spindle orientation even when dynein/dynactin is properly localized.

claim: NuMA's dynein-independent interactions with MTs are essential for spindle orientation.
source: Here, we have documented a new role for NuMA, one of the core components of the spindle orientation machinery. In addition to being important for the recruitment of dynein/dynactin to the cortex, we have found that NuMA's dynein-independent interactions with MTs are also essential for spindle orientation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spindle orientation defects in NuMAΔMTBD cells that maintain cortical dynein/dynactin.

claim: An unusual and previously unreported co-localization of NuMA with MT tips was reported.
source: We report an unusual and previously unreported co-localization of NuMA with MT tips and define a region within NuMA that is both necessary and sufficient for this localization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence showing NuMA at MT tips (Figures 1 and 2).

claim: A region within NuMA that is both necessary and sufficient for MT tip localization was defined.
source: We report an unusual and previously unreported co-localization of NuMA with MT tips and define a region within NuMA that is both necessary and sufficient for this localization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by localization studies of NuMA deletion constructs (Figure 2C-F).

claim: The properties of NuMA-TIP are distinct from many tip-binding proteins.
source: The properties of NuMA-TIP are distinct from many tip-binding proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NuMA-TIP remains on depolymerizing MTs, unlike typical +TIP proteins.

claim: NuMA-TIP remains associated with stalled and or depolymerizing MTs.
source: Most notably, NuMA-TIP remains associated with stalled and or depolymerizing MTs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging and nocodazole treatment experiments (Figures 1 and 2).

claim: There are very few proteins known to exhibit MT depolymerization-tracking behavior.
source: To date, there are very few proteins known to exhibit MT depolymerization-tracking behavior (either directly or indirectly).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The few known examples of depolymerization-tracking proteins are kinetochore proteins of different species, including the Dam1 complex, CENP-E, CENP-F, and the Ndc-80 complex.
source: The few known examples are kinetochore proteins of different species, including the Dam1 complex, CENP-E, CENP-F, and the Ndc-80 complex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Of the known depolymerization-tracking proteins, only Dam1 has been shown to follow depolymerizing MTs in vivo.
source: Of these, only Dam1 has been shown to follow depolymerizing MTs in vivo, while the others can do this in vitro, yet remain at the kinetochore-MT interface in vivo (Westermann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on a citation to previous research.

claim: Depolymerizing kinesins have been observed to localize to both plus and minus ends of MTs.
source: Depolymerizing kinesins have also been observed to localize to both plus and minus ends of MTs (Desai et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated based on a citation to previous research.

claim: A previous study demonstrated that artificially targeting dynein to the cortex was sufficient to induce spindle oscillations.
source: While a previous study demonstrated that artificially targeting dynein to the cortex was sufficient to induce spindle oscillations (Kotak et al., 2012), our data suggest that cortical dynein is not sufficient to robustly position the spindle and that NuMA-MT interactions are also required (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated based on a citation to previous research.

claim: Cortical dynein is not sufficient to robustly position the spindle and NuMA-MT interactions are also required.
source: While a previous study demonstrated that artificially targeting dynein to the cortex was sufficient to induce spindle oscillations (Kotak et al., 2012), our data suggest that cortical dynein is not sufficient to robustly position the spindle and that NuMA-MT interactions are also required (Figure 7).
evidence: This is concluded from the spindle orientation defects in NuMAΔMTBD cells with normal cortical dynein.

claim: Local taxol treatment at the posterior end of the C. elegans zygote prevented spindle movement toward that pole.
source: For example, local taxol treatment at the posterior end of the C. elegans zygote prevented spindle movement toward that pole (Nguyen-Ngoc et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on a citation to previous research.

claim: The spindle orientation process in yeast requires not only dynein-dependent pulling forces, but also MT depolymerization at the cell cortex.
source: Additionally, in contrast to the current model in metazoans, the spindle orientation process in yeast requires not only dynein-dependent pulling forces, but also MT depolymerization at the cell cortex (ten Hoopen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on a citation to previous research.

claim: NuMA's unique MT-binding qualities could allow it to interact with depolymerizing MTs and harness their energy to promote spindle rotation, thus collaborating with dynein pulling forces to robustly orient the spindle.
source: Alternatively, NuMA's unique MT-binding qualities revealed in this study could allow it to interact with depolymerizing MTs and harness their energy to promote spindle rotation, thus collaborating with dynein pulling forces to robustly orient the spindle.
evidence: This is proposed as a speculative model based on the data.

claim: This model is similar to kinetochores harnessing MT depolymerization for chromosome segregation.
source: This latter idea is similar to kinetochores harnessing MT depolymerization for chromosome segregation (McIntosh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an analogy to a known mechanism, supported by a citation.

claim: The association of MT dynamics with force generation observed during spindle positioning is consistent with NuMA harnessing MT depolymerization.
source: Both the association of MT dynamics with force generation observed during spindle positioning (Labbe et al., 2003), as well as work showing the ability of depolymerizing MTs to generate force (McIntosh et al., 2010) are consistent with this second possibility.
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous research.

claim: Positioning of the budding yeast spindle relies on regulated depolymerization at the cell cortex.
source: This is not without precedent, as positioning of the budding yeast spindle relies on regulated depolymerization at the cell cortex (Gupta et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on a citation to previous research.

claim: NuMA has been shown to collect at the minus ends of severed MTs in the mitotic spindle where it may act to stabilize the free ends.
source: For example, NuMA has been shown to collect at the minus ends of severed MTs in the mitotic spindle where it may act to stabilize the free ends (Elting et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on a citation to previous research.

claim: Loss of spindle orientation in the developing epidermis resulted in embryonic lethality that is likely due to epidermal differentiation defects.
source: Consistent with previous studies, loss of spindle orientation in the developing epidermis resulted in embryonic lethality that is likely due to epidermal differentiation defects.
evidence: This is concluded from the data showing differentiation defects and lethality (Figure 5).

claim: The phenotype that resulted from the epidermal-specific loss of NuMA's MTBD was less severe than that seen upon shRNA depletion of either LGN or NuMA.
source: While the phenotype that resulted from the epidermal-specific loss of NuMA's MTBD in this study was less severe than that seen upon shRNA depletion of either LGN or NuMA, there are two plausible explanations to reconcile this discrepancy.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with previous studies.

claim: The gene ablations in the previous study were initiated prior to epidermal stratification, whereas the knockout in this study occurred during the process of stratification.
source: First, the gene ablations in the previous study were initiated prior to epidermal stratification, whereas our knockout occured during the process of stratification.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for phenotypic differences.

claim: Loss of full-length NuMA or LGN resulted in a drastic conversion of ACDs (perpendicular spindles) to SCDs (parallel), while loss of NuMA's MTBD resulted in a conversion of ACDs to randomized division orientations.
source: Second, loss of full-length NuMA or LGN resulted in a drastic conversion of ACDs (perpendicular spindles) to SCDs (parallel), while loss of NuMA's MTBD resulted in a conversion of ACDs to randomized division orientations.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for phenotypic differences, based on data from this and previous studies.

claim: This is the first demonstration of an essential requirement for spindle orientation in hair follicle morphogenesis.
source: We have taken advantage of this by being the first to demonstrate an essential requirement for spindle orientation in hair follicle morphogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: Prior reports have presented correlative data to suggest that spindle orientation contributes to hair follicle morphogenesis.
source: While prior reports have presented correlative data to suggest that spindle orientation contributes to hair follicle morphogenesis (Niessen et al., 2013; Rompolas et al., 2012), we have quantitated division orientations within the rapidly proliferating matrix compartment and demonstrated the importance of spindle orientation in these cells.
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous research.

claim: Division orientations within the rapidly proliferating matrix compartment were quantitated and the importance of spindle orientation in these cells was demonstrated.
source: While prior reports have presented correlative data to suggest that spindle orientation contributes to hair follicle morphogenesis (Niessen et al., 2013; Rompolas et al., 2012), we have quantitated division orientations within the rapidly proliferating matrix compartment and demonstrated the importance of spindle orientation in these cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by spindle angle measurements and phenotypic analysis (Figure 6).

claim: Similar to the interfollicular epidermis in the embryo, divisions in the hair matrix can be either parallel or perpendicular to the underlying basement membrane.
source: Similar to the interfollicular epidermis in the embryo, divisions can be either parallel or perpendicular to the underlying basement membrane (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spindle orientation measurements in matrix cells (Figure 6G).

claim: The percentage of matrix cell perpendicular divisions decreased in the mutant and resulted in differentiation defects in matrix-derived lineages.
source: The percentage of matrix cell perpendicular divisions decreased in the mutant and resulted in differentiation defects in matrix-derived lineages.
evidence: This is demonstrated by spindle orientation measurements and loss of differentiation markers (Figure 6).

claim: Loss of BMP signaling resulted in phenotypes similar to loss of spindle orientation.
source: One of the earliest known steps of differentiation along these pathways is BMP activation (Andl et al., 2004; Kobielak et al., 2003; Kulessa et al., 2000), and loss of BMP signaling resulted in phenotypes similar to loss of spindle orientation.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison with previous research on BMP signaling.

claim: In both loss of spindle orientation and loss of BMP signaling, IRS and hair shaft markers are decreased or absent.
source: In both cases, IRS and hair shaft markers are decreased or absent.
evidence: This is stated as a similarity between the two conditions.

claim: The matrix-derived cells in the mutant mice as well as the BMPRIA mutant are non-proliferative.
source: The matrix-derived cells in the mutant mice described here as well as the BMPRIA mutant are non-proliferative, suggesting that they may be segregated from pro-proliferative signals from the basement membrane and/or dermal papilla.
evidence: This is stated based on BrdU incorporation data (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) and comparison with BMP mutants.

claim: In the absence of proper spindle orientation, the activation of BMP signaling does not occur.
source: Surprisingly, in the absence of proper spindle orientation, the activation of BMP signaling does not occur.
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of pSMAD1/5 staining in mutant follicles (Figure 6S,T).

claim: A reiterative use of spindle orientation machinery generates very distinct structures (stratified interfollicular epithelium versus hair follicles) within the same tissue.
source: In summary, we reveal that a reiterative use of spindle orientation machinery generates very distinct structures (stratified interfollicular epithelium versus hair follicles) within the same tissue.
evidence: This is concluded from the demonstration that spindle orientation is required in both embryonic epidermis and hair follicle matrix.
